text: Hey, thank you for a great question. No, I don't  think i've ever discussed in much detail what I   mean by that phrase, but I use it frequently and  so that's obviously a significant oversight on my
part. But I use it in a pretty broad sense to  refer to the influence of any of our important   social identities on our perception of,  reasoning through, or engagement with
different topics in public discourse. And I  think identity politics can run a spectrum from
good and constructive to bad and destructive,  and on the good end I would put those groups
who are marginalized and oppressed groups  who need to engage in this in order to   create and curate and defend identity markers and  boundaries in order to help their groups survive.
On the other end I would put the groups of  privilege and power who engage in different types
of structuring power to serve and advance their  own interests. And it's particularly destructive   when it is over and against the interests  of the other end of that spectrum. And so
within a religious studies context, I think  there are a lot of ways that Christians––who
have always had positions of privilege in  the United States–– have never experienced
criticism of certain assumptions and of certain  approaches. And so these things are so deeply
embedded in their intuitive cognition that they  can be quite––have quite a defensive and adverse
reaction to having them questioned, and can come  up with all different kinds of rationalizations
for why the things they've always taken for  granted ought to be more widely accepted. And
this one––that is one example: that we need to be  able to allow for true prophecy. Because you––you
know if you really interrogate these people  who are saying we have to allow for this. Well,   do we allow it also for the Quran? For the Book  of Mormon? Did Joseph Smith actually prophesy
of the Civil War? Or in those situations  with those groups that are not part of
your own social identity, can we then impose  those historical critical frameworks and say
that was very clearly not prophecy? when, when  it comes to the bible we have to presuppose it.
So um i would suggest that the folks who are kind  of reflexively reactively defend[ing] their own
world views without thinking critically about them  are engaged in identity politics, and if they––if
they are situated on the side of that  spectrum that is more susceptible to corrosive   and destructive identity politics, I say  they probably need to think twice about that.
